title: How to Make ASCII Art: 22 FIGlet Fonts, Spacing and CJK Limits
description: ASCII art generator guide: 22 FIGlet fonts in 4 groups, 40–200 column widths, CJK pixel art with 3 charsets, and image-to-ASCII rows set by aspect ratio.
content:
The site's ASCII art tool makes an English banner in three steps: choose “English Banner”, type letters or digits, and wait about 250 ms for the automatic render. Change the font, the spacing or the line width and it redraws; Chinese has no FIGlet font, so input containing it falls back to pixel-art rendering.

1. The short answer: three steps to a first piece of ASCII art

All three tabs share one “Terminal Output” block: English banners go through FIGlet, while CJK pixel art samples character by character. Switching tabs redraws immediately from the current input; if you switch to image mode with no image chosen, pressing “Generate ASCII Art” is what tells you to select an image first.

The top of the output panel is a fake command line, the art sits below it, and the top right shows “max width × rows”; the status bar gives 「生成完成」 (“Generation complete”) or an error message. The stats line counts “N 行 · M 字符 · 最大宽度 W” (“N lines · M characters · max width W”), and M includes the newlines: Standard output for CLOVER TOOLS is 10 lines of 38 characters, and 380 plus 9 newlines gives 389.

2. 22 fonts in four groups: how to read the “glyph” figure in the hint

The font dropdown is not 22 flat options but 4 optgroups: 8 classic fonts (Standard, Slant, Banner, Big, Block, Small, Mini, Calvin S), 7 cool fonts, 4 3D fonts and 3 decorative fonts. Each entry is a Chinese display name plus the font name in brackets, Standard is selected by default, and after a change the hint line becomes “display name · description · glyph max width × height”.

The “glyph 16×6” in the hint comes from figlet.metadata: 16 is the widest single character in the font and 6 is the font height, not the final output's width and height. Fonts differ widely: Mini is 10×4, Calvin S is 7×3 and Poison is 20×12; for the same input “CLOVER”, Standard prints 6 lines with a max width of 38, while Poison stretches to 24 lines and a max width of 50.

The same text in another font changes both row count and width, so pick by purpose first: Mini, Small or Calvin S for comments and short phrases; Banner, Big or ANSI Shadow for headings; 3D-ASCII, Larry 3D or Big Money-ne when you want depth. The tool card says “21 FIGlet English fonts”, but the page actually loads 22 .flf files (8+7+4+3), and this article follows the page's options.

3. Spacing and line width: why one sentence breaks into two blocks

Spacing maps to figlet's horizontalLayout; the four options are “Default (font-designed)”, “Compact”, “Wide” and “Universal”, sending default, fitted, full and universal respectively. Default uses the spacing the font's author designed; Compact pushes letters until they almost touch; Wide keeps the full character cells. Changing the font, the spacing or the width redraws.

The Universal option needs a note: it sends universal to figlet, while figlet.js documents universal smushing as the legal value. In the browser evidence, the Universal output is identical to Default character for character, and the command line still reads -l universal, so the option has no real effect; for tighter or looser spacing, use fitted or full.

Line width offers 40/60/80/120/160/200, default 60, and is passed to figlet as width together with whitespaceBreak, so lines break at whitespace. Take the text “CLOVER TOOLS CLOVER TOOLS”: at width 40 it folds into 18 lines with a max width of 38, and at width 120 it packs back into 10 lines with a max width of 107. A very long word has no whitespace to break at, so a single line can still run past the setting.

4. What happens when you type Chinese: the switch to pixel art

The FIGlet fonts cover mainly ASCII and contain no Chinese glyphs. The page tests the input with one CJK_RE: as soon as a CJK unified ideograph, Hangul, kana, full-width punctuation or a full-width letter appears, it skips FIGlet and calls the CJK pixel-art renderer directly.

The tab does not move to “CJK Pixel Art”; it stays on “English Banner” and only the output changes. The font choice is ignored, resolution is fixed at 8 rows per character, the charset is grayscale and invert is off, and the width follows “Line Width”. The status bar turns into a blue info notice saying that a CJK or full-width character was detected, that CJK pixel art was used for rendering, and that the resolution can be adjusted in that mode.

For example, type 中文 (“Chinese”) into the English input box and the output is 8 lines with a max width of 32; switch the font to Slant, type the same characters, and the output is identical character for character. To adjust resolution, charset or invert, you have to switch to “CJK Pixel Art” and render again.

5. The four CJK pixel-art parameters and the font dependency

“Resolution” is 6/8/10/12 rows per character, default 8. Each character is first drawn to a canvas at bold ${res×4}px — 24, 32, 40 and 48 px for 6, 8, 10 and 12 rows — and then sampled on a 2×4 pixel grid; 8 rows per character is a 32 px glyph height and 12 rows is 48 px. The larger the font size, the more stroke detail and the more output rows: the sample input (the product's Chinese name on one line, CloverTools on the next) at 8 rows per character, grayscale and width 60 comes out at 30 lines, and at 12 rows per character with invert still off it reaches 62 lines.

The charset has three levels: fine grayscale .:-=+*#%@ (10 levels), high-contrast blocks ░▒▓█ (5 levels) and binary dots # (2 levels). After sampling, the pixel is alpha-composited onto white and its luminance is taken as 0.299R+0.587G+0.114B; when not inverted, ink is 255 minus luminance, then gamma 0.65 boosts thin strokes, and finally the index is ink/256×charset.length, rounded down. The darker the stroke, the denser the character.

Invert swaps ink for luminance itself, so the background becomes a field of @ or #, the glyphs turn hollow, and the output often has more lines and reads like a white-on-black negative. Line breaks accumulate the pixel widths from measureText and break once they pass “width × 2 pixels”, so the column count is not a fixed grid: the same text comes out differently across systems depending on whether Noto Sans SC, Microsoft YaHei or PingFang is installed. When drawing ends, blank lines at the top and bottom are trimmed, trailing spaces are removed, and consecutive newlines are collapsed.

6. Image to ASCII: columns decide rows, contrast only changes light and dark

Image mode accepts PNG/JPG/GIF/WebP, by click or by drag; it only checks whether file.type begins with image/, and other types get a prompt to choose an image file (PNG / JPG / GIF / WebP), while a decode failure reports that the image failed to load and asks for another file. Once a file is chosen, the preview shows “file name · width×height” and the size in B/KB/MB.

Output width is 60/80/100/120/160 columns, and the row count follows from the image's proportions: rows = max(1, round(cols × height / width)). A 200×100 image at 60 columns gives 30 rows, and at 80 columns 40 rows; each character covers 2×4 pixels (2 across, 4 down), so detail is coarser than the original. A monospace character in the terminal is roughly twice as tall as it is wide, so the grid's on-screen height comes out at about 2 × (image height / image width) times its width: a 200×100 landscape image at 60 columns becomes 60×30, close to square on screen and stretched vertically, and the page applies no aspect-ratio compensation. Removing the image brings the drop zone back, clears the output and the status line, and leaves the parameters as they are; but the preview block only receives the hidden attribute, and display:flex in the stylesheet keeps it visible, so the old file name and size stay on the page and the image turns into a broken-image icon; to change images cleanly, use “Choose again”.

Contrast runs 0–200% with a default of 100%; the formula is (luminance−128)×contrast+128 clamped to 0–255. Lower values wash the picture toward gray, higher ones separate black from white. Invert flips light and dark, and the three charsets are the same as in CJK pixel art. Every cell also keeps the RGB it sampled, so with ANSI color on it is colored cell by cell.

7. ANSI color, copy and download: the terminal is only a preview

“Terminal Output” is a simulator: buildCommand assembles the command line; English mode writes figlet -f Standard -l default -w 60 "CLOVER TOOLS", CJK mode writes clover-ascii "三叶草工具箱" -res 8 -charset gray -w 60, and image mode writes img2txt "filename" -w 60 -charset gray; -c is added only when contrast is not 100%, and -invert only when invert is on. None of these commands is actually executed, and there is no shell.

With ANSI color ticked, text mode colors line by line: hue runs linearly from 40° to 300°, one 24-bit truecolor escape (\x1b[38;2;r;g;bm) per line; image mode colors cell by cell with each cell's sampled RGB. The terminal preview renders colored spans, and the copy carries the escapes as well, so pasting into a terminal that supports them shows the colors; text mode colors by line, not by character.

Download is always plain text: the Blob holds only the art, the filename is fixed as clover-ascii-art-YYYYMMDD.txt, and the ANSI checkbox does not affect it. With no result, copy reports that there is nothing to copy and asks you to generate art first, and download reports that there is nothing to download and asks the same; “Clear” wipes the input, the output and the status together but keeps the current mode and parameters.

8. Common errors and a self-check list

Four problems come up most often: treating the simulated terminal's command line as something that really ran; typing Chinese and finding the font options do nothing; switching modes and seeing the output cleared; and downloading plain text when a colored picture was expected.

  • English banner only: check the tab is “English Banner”, keep the input to ASCII, and start from width 60.
  • Chinese turns into pixel art: this is the automatic fallback, not a broken font; to adjust resolution, switch to “CJK Pixel Art”.
  • “Universal” changes nothing: figlet only recognizes universal smushing, so this option equals Default.
  • Output disappears on a mode switch: switching to an empty CJK mode clears it and shows a hint immediately; image mode only hints after you press “Generate ASCII Art”. Switching back to English redraws from the current input.
  • Copy comes out colored: with ANSI color ticked, the copy carries ESC sequences; untick it first for plain text.
  • Download has no color: the .txt is always plain text, and color exists only in the terminal preview and in copied content.

The self-check order: first whether the tab and the input box match, then whether the status bar is a success, a hint or an error, and finally whether the stats line matches expectations. When the output width clearly exceeds the setting, check for an over-long word first, then whether the font is simply wide. To work on the result further, the Text Case Converter can normalize case or full-width/half-width characters; to check the fonts and canvas capabilities the browser exposes, see Browser Info.

9. Limits and sources

FIGlet only works with the characters a font contains; Chinese, Japanese, Korean and emoji are all absent from the 22 .flf files. Chinese goes to pixel art automatically, but emoji is not in CJK_RE, so it falls into the FIGlet branch and produces an empty string, with no error message. Pixel-art width depends on the system fonts, so the same text can differ across systems; image mode only maps light and dark and does not recognize content. The output is text, not an image; the terminal is a simulator and cannot execute commands. For short signals that can be decoded, see the Morse code tool, which likewise only maps character by character.

Sources: the FIGlet project page and the Wikipedia entry cover FIGlet's history and font mechanism; the figlet.js repository documents width, whitespaceBreak, horizontalLayout and metadata; MDN explains that measureText returns text width, and that getImageData and canvas pixel manipulation read canvas pixels. The fonts, groups, defaults and wording in this article follow the page source and the browser evidence gathered in this round.

faqs.q: How do I generate ASCII art?
faqs.a: Open ASCII art, make sure the tab is “English Banner”, type letters or digits into the input box, and the result appears automatically after about 250 ms; you can also press “Generate ASCII Art” or Ctrl+Enter to render immediately. Changes to the font, spacing or line width redraw automatically, the output lands in the “Terminal Output” panel below, and the stats line gives “N lines · M characters · max width W”.

faqs.q: Why do the font options do nothing after I type Chinese?
faqs.a: Because the FIGlet fonts have no Chinese glyphs. As soon as the input matches CJK_RE (Chinese, kana, Hangul, full-width characters), the page skips FIGlet and uses a fixed pixel-art path at 8 rows per character, grayscale and no invert, and shows a blue hint; the tab stays on “English Banner” and the font choice is ignored. To adjust resolution, charset or invert, switch to “CJK Pixel Art” and render again.

faqs.q: Why is “Universal” spacing the same as Default?
faqs.a: The page passes the option as universal, while the legal value in the figlet.js documentation is universal smushing. In this round's browser evidence, the Universal output is identical to Default character for character, and the command line still reads -l universal, so it has no effect; for tighter or looser output, use Compact (fitted) or Wide (full).

faqs.q: Why does the width of CJK pixel art change from run to run?
faqs.a: It wraps by the actual pixel width from measureText, with a threshold of “line width × 2 pixels”, not a fixed character grid. The font stack is made of system fonts such as Noto Sans SC, Microsoft YaHei and PingFang, so installations differ and the width and shape of the same character differ too; add 2×4 sampling, trimmed blank lines and stripped trailing spaces, and the final column count varies by system.

faqs.q: How is the row count of image-to-ASCII calculated?
faqs.a: The row count follows the image's aspect ratio and the output column count: rows = max(1, round(cols × height / width)). A 200×100 image at 60 columns is 30 rows, and at 80 columns 40 rows; each character averages a 2×4 pixel cell, and monospace cells are about twice as tall as they are wide, so the rendered block stretches vertically (a 200×100 image at 60 columns becomes a near-square 60×30 block); the page applies no aspect-ratio compensation. Contrast only changes light and dark, never the rows or columns.

faqs.q: What is the difference between copy and download?
faqs.a: With “ANSI color” ticked, copy writes 24-bit truecolor escape sequences into the clipboard, colored by line in text mode and by cell in image mode; download always writes plain text with the fixed filename clover-ascii-art-YYYYMMDD.txt. With no result, copy reports that there is nothing to copy and asks you to generate art first, and download reports that there is nothing to download and asks the same.

focus: Three paths through the ASCII art tool: FIGlet English banners (22 fonts in 4 groups, spacing and width), CJK pixel art (6–12 rows per character, 3 charsets, invert) and image-to-ASCII (60–160 columns, row count from the aspect ratio, contrast and per-cell ANSI). Chinese has no FIGlet font and falls back to pixel art automatically; pixel-art width depends on system fonts, and emoji returns an empty string.
